pgb1q1-cadanl.summary: Opens the literal exposition at the prologue's incipit 'Cupientes aliquid'. Gracilis makes the first division of the whole Book of Sentences into a prologue and a treatise, and places the start of the treatise at 'veteris ac novae legis' (d. 1).
claims: The Book of Sentences divides into a prologue and a treatise.
The treatise begins at 'veteris ac novae legis'.

pgb1q1-ppdlde.summary: Divides the prologue into four principal parts, each given its incipit. They are the author's excuse in undertaking the work, his rebuke of envious detractors, his commendation of the work, and his exhortation to hearers to make progress.
claims: The prologue has four principal parts: excuse of the author, rebuke of the envious, commendation of the work, and exhortation of the hearers.

pgb1q1-ppddis.summary: Subdivides the first part as a contest of motives. Three causes hold Lombard back: the slenderness of his knowledge, the arduousness of the subject, and the bite of envy. Three urge him on: the example of the poor widow, the hope of eternal reward, and the persistent requests of his companions. A final section shows the motivating causes winning. The last cause is itself divided into the evidence of the opponents' contradiction, its cause, and the opponents' wickedness.
claims: Lombard weighs three restraining causes against three motivating causes, and the motivating causes prevail.

pgb1q1-tssiqp.summary: Divides the second principal part ('quamvis non ambigamus'). It rebukes the detractors twice over: for attacking the truth and for teaching falsehood.
claims: The rebuke of the detractors concerns both their attack on truth and their teaching of falsehood.

pgb1q1-sepicl.summary: Divides the third principal part ('horum igitur'). Gracilis reads it as commending the work through its four Aristotelian causes in turn (final, efficient, material, formal) and locates where each begins.
claims: Lombard commends the work by its final, efficient, material and formal causes.

pgb1q1-tsqigp.summary: Divides the fourth and last principal part ('non ergo debet hic labor'). The hearer is spurred on by the work's useful brevity, its humble truth, and its exposure of evident falsehood. This completes the general division of the prologue.
claims: The hearer is motivated by the brevity, the truth and the anti-heretical usefulness of the work.

pgb1q1-isvioa.summary: Begins the specific exposition (in speciali), following Lombard's order of argument rather than the schematic division. Lombard pairs each motive with its opposite: desire to profit others against lack of talent and knowledge, and the height of the subject and size of the labour against confidence in divine help and Christ's promised reward. Ardent love for the Church then overcomes the obstacles.
claims: Lombard's love for the Church overcomes his reasons for declining the work.

pgb1q1-iapipv.summary: Completes the specific exposition and leads into the question. Lombard's intention covers three things: defending the Catholic faith, explaining theological truth, and setting out the sacraments. The brothers' requests motivate him and the envious oppose him. Their opposition is traced to a disordered will, from which error arises, from error envy, and from envy contradiction. Their wickedness is to subordinate reason and Scripture to their own opinion under a feigned religiosity, chasing novelty. Gracilis then gives the work's causes. The final cause is twofold: overturning falsehood and showing Catholic truth. The efficient cause is God as principal and the Master as instrument. The material cause is the testimonies of canons and saints. The formal cause is twofold: the forma tractatus (books and chapters) and the forma tractandi (mode of proceeding).
claims: The efficient cause of the Sentences is God principally and Lombard instrumentally.
The material cause is the testimonies of truth from the canons and saints.
The formal cause is twofold: forma tractatus and forma tractandi.
Contradiction of the truth arises from a disordered will through error and envy.

pgb1q1-uqvovs.summary: States the prologue question. Can a wayfarer (viator), without a special gift, give scientific theological assent to every supernatural truth? The question carries forward the prologue's contrast between the arduousness of the matter and human capacity.

pgb1q1-qspali.summary: First principal argument for the affirmative. Every natural power can attain its natural operation, and the intellect's operation is knowing, so it can assent without infused faith or light. Confirmation: if reason alone yields assent to one truth, it yields assent to any, since all truths act on the intellect under a single ratio, as every sensible is equally knowable to sense.
claims: A natural power can reach its natural act without supernatural aid.
All truths have the same ratio of moving the intellect.

pgb1q1-shdsam.summary: Second principal argument. Heretics, the damned, and the devil assent to theological truths without any special light, as the rich man of Luke 16 shows, so a wayfarer can too. Also, when agent and patient are sufficiently applied, action follows. The agent intellect can make all things and the possible intellect become all things, so assent follows naturally.
claims: Those lacking grace can still assent to theological truths.
The agent and possible intellects suffice for any intellection.

pgb1q1-tsqpap.summary: Third principal argument, by reductio. If the negative were true, every theologian would have a special light infused. But no modern theologian perceives such an infusion, and, following Thomas of Strasbourg, such lights or habits cannot be present without their possessor noticing.
claims: Infused habits cannot be hidden from their possessor.
No theologian perceives an infused theological light.

pgb1q1-qvprit.summary: Fourth principal argument. Reason alone can prove a future life, which is a theological truth. Humans are ordered to final rest no less than a stone to its natural place. Nothing in this life gives such rest, so another life must exist. Augustine's 'inquietum est cor nostrum' supports this.
claims: Natural reason can demonstrate a future life from the natural desire for rest.

pgb1q1-ioeqqv.summary: Sed contra, from authority. Augustine says Scripture's authority exceeds all human acuity, and that whatever is true in the soul's reasoning belongs to the light of truth rather than to the soul. Lombard admits his work exceeds his powers. Augustine also holds that no created wisdom is gained without illumination by grace.
claims: Theological truth exceeds unaided human ingenuity.
Created wisdom requires divine illumination.

pgb1q1-pclecv.summary: First conclusion, which lays the semantic groundwork. A theological assent is not distinct from the theological proposition, since otherwise one could assent without complex knowledge. Yet two propositions with the same subject and predicate, signifying the same, can differ in species. When a believer and an unbeliever both form 'Christ suffered', the believer's proposition is intrinsically an assent and the unbeliever's is not.
claims: Theological assent is identical with the theological (mental) proposition.
Propositions with the same terms can differ in species according to whether they are assents.

pgb1q1-pcqnet.summary: First corollary: one could know all of Scripture and not be a theologian, as an unbeliever who knows it but does not assent. Gracilis defines infidelity as assent to falsehood, or dissent from truth, that the Church has determined or Scripture has revealed.
claims: Knowing Scripture without assent does not make one a theologian.
Infidelity is assent to falsehood or dissent from truth determined by the Church or revealed in Scripture.

pgb1q1-scqeeh.summary: Second corollary: a wayfarer may be informed by the theological habit without being called a theologian. Under the ordained law the habit that is theology can persist without faith, but without faith it does not remain theology. Being theological is therefore less essential to the theological habit than being a habit.
claims: The theological habit can exist without faith, but then it does not count as theology.
Being theological is not as essential to the habit as being a habit.

pgb1q1-tcqdia.summary: Third corollary: one proposition, indistinct in its terms, can have two contradictories distinct in species. The contradictory may be an assent in one mind and a dissent in another.
claims: One proposition can have specifically distinct contradictories.

pgb1q1-scqsot.summary: Second conclusion. A theological proposition is theological cognition, but no knowledge is its own total object. Faith requires assent, and by the first conclusion assent is the proposition, so the proposition is the cognition. Knowledge is caused at least partly by its object, and nothing causes itself. Even a vision that saw itself would need another object to cause it.
claims: A theological proposition is theological cognition.
No knowledge is its own total object, since knowledge is partly caused by its object.

pgb1q1-pcqoss.summary: First corollary of the second conclusion: theological propositions are not the object of Sacred Scripture (theology).
claims: Theological propositions are not the object of Sacred Scripture.

pgb1q1-scqste.summary: Second corollary: theology, like any science, is not properly what is known but that by which something is known. What is known is a science's object, and a science is not its own total object.
claims: A science is that by which something is known, not what is known.

pgb1q1-tcqvne.summary: Third corollary: taken strictly (de virtute sermonis), 'Socrates knows grammar (logic, theology)' is false, because a science is not what is known but that by which things are known to be or not to be so.
claims: 'Socrates knows theology' is false de virtute sermonis.

pgb1q1-tclsie.summary: Third conclusion, which answers the question directly. It is not contradictory for a wayfarer to have the habit and even the act of faith while believing no theological truth: habits exist without operation, and God could separate the act from its actuating as he separates an accident from its inherence. But under the present law a wayfarer cannot assent to theological truths without a special light. Augustine (Ep. 120; In Ioh. tr. 1) and Anselm (Cur Deus homo) are cited for this.
claims: The act and habit of faith can exist without actually believing any truth.
Under the present law, assent to theological truths requires a special light.

pgb1q1-pcpiss.summary: First corollary: many will be saved who never actually believed, such as infants who die right after baptism and baptized persons who never had the use of reason.
claims: Salvation does not require actual belief.

pgb1q1-scmiss.summary: Second corollary: many in heaven would have been damned had they believed. Greek infants are validly baptized despite a different form of words and receive saving grace, but die before the age of discretion. Adult Greeks, who believe otherwise than the Roman Church, are not in a state of salvation.
claims: Greek baptism confers saving grace.
Adult Greeks dissenting from the Roman Church are not in a state of salvation.

pgb1q1-tchnqv.summary: Third corollary: under the present law a wayfarer can fail to believe as the Church commands without sinning, because one may licitly believe nothing for a time. Gracilis concludes that the negative answer to the question is true.
claims: One can licitly believe nothing for a time.
The question is to be answered in the negative.

pgb1q1-cpceia.summary: First objection, against the first conclusion. An unbeliever can form every proposition a believer forms while lacking theological assent. So a theological proposition can exist without assent and is distinct from it.
claims: Any proposition a believer forms can be formed by an unbeliever.

pgb1q1-ssqsqp.summary: Second objection. On Gracilis's view, a theologian who became a heretic would lose all theological science. That is false, since he could still defend the faith, lecture, dispute, and answer arguments as before.
claims: A heretical theologian retains his theological skill.

pgb1q1-tpaeca.summary: Third objection. Through an assent we assent to a proposition, so the assent is not the proposition. Otherwise that by which we assent and that to which we assent would be the same.
claims: What we assent by differs from what we assent to.

pgb1q1-qsiepm.summary: Fourth objection. The same proposition can remain while assent to it ceases, as when someone changes their mind for reasons. So proposition and assent are distinct.
claims: A proposition can persist through loss of assent.

pgb1q1-qcstss.summary: Fifth objection, against the second part of the first conclusion. If assent diversified a proposition's species, no one dissenting from 'no man is an ass' could form a proposition of the same species. Yet he forms one with the same subject and predicate, and propositions are nothing beyond their terms taken together.
claims: A proposition is nothing beyond its terms taken together.

pgb1q1-sccqrd.summary: Sixth objection, against the corollaries on faith and theology. If they are one habit, having the theological habit makes one a theologian. If they are distinct, suppose both decline uniformly toward non-being. If they cease together they are equal, contradicting Augustine (De Trin. XIV) that theology surpasses faith. If not, theology outlasts faith, contradicting what was said.
claims: Faith and theology are either one habit or two, and either option causes trouble for Gracilis.

pgb1q1-scsons.summary: Seventh objection, against the second part of the second conclusion. Everything known is true and only propositions are true, so only a proposition is known and only a proposition is the total object of science.
claims: Only propositions are true, so only propositions are known.

pgb1q1-occrea.summary: Eighth objection, against the corollaries of the second conclusion. The total object of theology is either the proposition, the extramental thing, or the signified. The first contradicts the first corollary. The second would make sciences concern contingent things, against Aristotle. The third reduces to the second, since a proposition signifies an extramental thing. Confirmation: then one and the same God would be object of knowledge, opinion, faith, and error at once.
claims: The object of theology must be a proposition, an external thing, or the significate, and each option fails.

pgb1q1-nctiec.summary: Ninth objection, against the third conclusion. Theological truths are self-evident or deduced from self-evident truths, so faith is not needed to know them. One is bound to believe without doubt only what is per se notum, and every truth is virtually contained in a first principle.
claims: All truths are deducible from a first principle.
Theological truths are per se nota or derived from such.

pgb1q1-dstogd.summary: Tenth objection. If such a light were required, everyone would be bound to a certainty about these truths greater than scientific certainty, since the certainty of faith would be infinitely removed from all doubt. That is false.
claims: The certainty of faith would have to be infinite.

pgb1q1-unlfdm.summary: Eleventh objection. No special light is needed to assent to a lie. Someone who states a theological truth he thinks false is lying, so none is needed for assent to theological truth either.
claims: Assent to a lie requires no special light.

pgb1q1-arasap.summary: Reply to the first objection. Gracilis distinguishes two senses of 'theological proposition': any proposition signifying a theological matter (even a spoken one), and a proposition that is intrinsically a theological assent. In the second sense it cannot exist without assent. The unbeliever forms theological propositions only in the first sense.
claims: 'Theological proposition' is ambiguous between signifying theological matter and being a theological assent.

pgb1q1-ascddt.summary: Reply to the second objection. Gracilis concedes that the apostate loses theological science if science includes assent. If science is taken as a habit of inferring one proposition from another, he keeps it, but should not be called a theologian.
claims: An apostate keeps the inferential habit but loses the title of theologian.

pgb1q1-atnepr.summary: Reply to the third objection. The assent is the very proposition by which we assent, and what we assent to is not the proposition but that things are or are not so (sic esse vel non sic esse).
claims: The object of assent is the state of affairs (sic esse), not the proposition.

pgb1q1-aqnnmp.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. While the assent lasts, so does the proposition. What can remain after assent ceases is a similar proposition that is not an assent and so not theological. The theological proposition does not itself remain.
claims: When assent ceases, the theological proposition ceases, though a similar non-assenting proposition may remain.

pgb1q1-aqcssa.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. Gracilis concedes the consequent and denies the inference. An assenting proposition includes, beyond its terms, the assent itself. Alternatively, the copulas differ in species, because one joins subject and predicate assentingly and the other by mere apprehension.
claims: An assenting proposition includes more than its terms.
The copula of an assent differs in species from that of an apprehension.

pgb1q1-asdqas.summary: Reply to the sixth objection. Faith and theology are not one habit. Granting the case of uniform remission, some degree of the theological habit would remain, but without faith it would not, under the present law, make its possessor theological. Gracilis notes that Alphonsus Vargas identifies the two habits while Thomas of Strasbourg distinguishes them and answers his arguments.
claims: Faith and theology are distinct habits.
Without faith, the theological habit does not denominate its possessor a theologian.

pgb1q1-asqqpf.summary: Reply to the seventh objection. Gracilis denies that only propositions are true. The significates of propositions are true too, as Aristotle's treatment of opposites in the Categories implies. They are called true by extrinsic denomination, as what a true proposition signifies or would signify. Or they are true by the first truth, God, who is the true and certain judgment of all of them.
claims: The significates of propositions are true by extrinsic denomination.
All true signifiables are true by reference to the first truth, God.

pgb1q1-aodsht.summary: Reply to the eighth objection. The object of science is none of the proposed options. It is that things are or are not so (sic esse vel non esse), which is a res only in the broad sense of anything complexly or incomplexly signifiable. Sciences concern necessary things not because their objects are necessary entities (only God is), but because what is known cannot be otherwise: if something is an isosceles triangle, it has angles equal to two right angles. On the confirmation, Gracilis concedes that one can know, believe, and err about the same God under diverse considerations.
claims: The object of science is the complexly signifiable 'sic esse vel non esse'.
Scientific necessity is conditional necessity of the known, not the necessary existence of things.
The same God can be known, believed, and erred about under different considerations.

pgb1q1-aanpap.summary: Reply to the ninth objection. Gracilis denies that theological truths are self-evident to wayfarers. The objection's major premise holds only if 'per se notum' means held on account of nothing more certain, which is how William of Auxerre can call the articles of faith per se nota. He refers to Hugolino of Orvieto for the distinctions of per se notum.
claims: Theological truths are not self-evident to wayfarers.
'Per se notum' has a weaker sense in which the articles may be so called.

pgb1q1-aanafi.summary: Reply to the tenth objection. The certainty of faith is not infinite. No created certainty is, since each is a finite act or a habit inclining to a finite act.
claims: No created certainty is infinite.

pgb1q1-aunqev.summary: Reply to the eleventh objection. Sometimes one must believe a lie without hesitation, not as a lie, but because the speaker says what he thinks false while it is in fact true. So faith's assent to such a statement is not assent to a lie as such.
claims: One may be bound to believe a statement that is a lie on the speaker's part but true in fact.

pgb1q1-aprpqq.summary: Reply to the first principal argument. Gracilis concedes the major and the indefinite conclusion, that the intellect can naturally know something. He denies the confirmation's inferences, since not all truths move the intellect equally or in the same way. He refers to Henry of Ghent.
claims: The intellect can naturally know some truths.
Truths do not move the intellect equally or in the same manner.

pgb1q1-aaqinc.summary: Reply to the second principal argument. The principle that applied agent and patient produce action holds for a total and precise agent. The agent intellect is not the total cause of intellection, so the argument fails.
claims: The agent intellect is only a partial cause of intellection.

pgb1q1-aacpsp.summary: Reply to the third principal argument. Gracilis concedes that every theologian has the special light and denies that it must be perceived. By the same reasoning there would be no infused charity or grace, since those who have them do not perceive them and no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred. Alternatively, every theologian perceives the light, but imperfectly and without perceiving that he perceives it.
claims: Infused habits need not be perceived by their possessor.
Every theologian has the special light.

pgb1q1-aupqef.summary: Reply to the fourth principal argument. Even if reason could argue for a future life without the special light, it cannot do so in the manner or with the perfection of faith or theology. The same answer applies to the first argument.
claims: Natural reason cannot reach theological truths with the certainty proper to faith.

pg-b1q1-d1e1266.summary: Alternative reply to the fourth principal argument. Gracilis denies the antecedent: the proofs offered do not demonstrate a future life. By parity they would prove that man can attain beatitude from purely natural powers, which is false.
claims: Natural-desire arguments do not demonstrate a future life.
Man cannot attain beatitude from purely natural powers.

pg-b1q1-Dd1e3724.summary: Literal exposition (circa textum) of Lombard's prologue. Gracilis first divides the Sentences into prologue and treatise, then the prologue into four parts: the author's excuse, the rebuke of envious detractors, the commendation of the work, and the exhortation of hearers. Each part is subdivided with incipits. The excuse is read as a contest of motives, in which Lombard's diffidence about his knowledge and the arduous matter gives way to zeal for the Church, divine aid, and his brothers' requests. The specific exposition then traces the detractors' opposition to a disordered will (error, envy, contradiction) and presents the work through its four causes, with God as principal and Lombard as instrumental efficient cause. The section closes by introducing the question, which picks up the prologue's theme of the gap between theological matter and human capacity.
claims: The prologue divides into excuse, rebuke, commendation, and exhortation.
The Sentences has God as principal and Lombard as instrumental efficient cause.
Opposition to truth springs from a disordered will through error and envy.

pg-b1q1-Dd1e3928.summary: Principal arguments. Four arguments hold that a wayfarer can assent to theological truths without a special gift. The intellect is a natural power able to reach any truth. Heretics, the damned, and demons assent without grace, and the agent and possible intellects suffice for any intellection. No theologian perceives an infused light, which could not be hidden. Reason alone proves a future life from the natural desire for rest. The sed contra cites Augustine and Lombard: Scripture's authority exceeds human ingenuity, and true wisdom requires illumination by grace.
claims: Arguments for: the intellect's natural sufficiency, the belief of those without grace, the imperceptibility of any infused light, and natural proof of a future life.
Against: theological truth requires divine illumination.

pg-b1q1-Dd1e4089.summary: First conclusion and corollaries, setting out the semantics of theological assent. Theological assent is identical with the mental proposition, yet propositions with the same terms differ in species according to whether they are assents, as with the believer's and unbeliever's 'Christ suffered'. It follows that knowing Scripture without assent does not make one a theologian. Infidelity is dissent from what the Church has determined or Scripture revealed. The theological habit can persist without faith but then does not count as theology. One proposition can have specifically distinct contradictories.
claims: Theological assent is identical with the theological proposition.
Same-term propositions differ in species as assent or non-assent.
Without faith one is not a theologian, whatever one's knowledge of Scripture.

pg-b1q1-Dd1e4123.summary: Second conclusion and corollaries, on cognition and its object. The theological proposition is theological cognition, but no cognition is its own total object, since knowledge is partly caused by its object. So theological propositions are not the object of Scripture. A science is that by which something is known rather than what is known, and 'Socrates knows theology' is strictly false.
claims: A theological proposition is theological cognition.
No cognition is its own total object.
A science is id quo, not id quod, of knowledge.

pg-b1q1-Dd1e4151.summary: Third conclusion and corollaries, which answer the question. One can have the habit and even the act of faith while actually believing nothing, but under the present law a wayfarer cannot assent to theological truths without a special light, as Augustine and Anselm attest. So salvation does not require actual belief, as with baptized infants and those without reason. Baptized Greek infants are saved although adult Greeks dissenting from Rome are not. One may licitly not believe as the Church commands for a time. The question is answered in the negative.
claims: Under the present law, theological assent requires a special light.
Salvation does not require actual belief.
The question's answer is negative.

pg-b1q1-Doeroer.summary: Eleven objections against the three conclusions. Against the first: an unbeliever can form any believer's proposition; a lapsed theologian keeps his skill; what we assent by differs from what we assent to; a proposition can survive loss of assent; propositions are nothing beyond their terms; and a dilemma about whether faith and theology are one habit. Against the second: only propositions are true and known, and the object of theology must be a proposition, an external thing, or a significate, each of which fails. Against the third: theological truths are self-evident or deducible; a special light would make faith's certainty infinite; and assent to a lie needs no special light.

pg-b1q1-Dd1e1073.summary: Replies to the objections and the principal arguments. Gracilis distinguishes signifying-theological from assenting-theological propositions. He separates the inferential habit, which an apostate keeps, from theology properly so called. The object of assent and of science is the complexe significabile 'sic esse vel non esse', true by extrinsic denomination or by reference to God as first truth. Scientific necessity is conditional, as in the isosceles example. Faith and theology are distinct habits. The articles are not self-evident to wayfarers, and no created certainty is infinite. Against the principal arguments: truths do not move the intellect equally; the agent intellect is not a total cause; infused habits, like grace, need not be perceived; and natural arguments for a future life lack faith's certainty or fail outright, since they would also prove natural beatitude.
claims: The object of assent and of science is 'sic esse vel non esse'.
Faith and theology are distinct habits.
Infused habits need not be perceived by their possessors.
Natural reason cannot reach theological truths with the certainty of faith.

pg-b1q1-Dd1e3922.summary: Gracilis's prologue question asks whether a wayfarer can, without a special gift, give scientific theological assent to every supernatural truth. The principal arguments appeal to the natural sufficiency of the intellect, the belief of heretics and demons, the imperceptibility of any infused light, and natural proof of a future life. Three conclusions build the answer. First, theological assent is identical with the mental proposition, and same-term propositions differ in species according to whether they are assents, so knowledge of Scripture without faith does not make a theologian. Second, a science is that by which things are known, not its own object. Third, under the present law theological assent requires a special light, though the habit of faith can exist without actual belief. The replies set out a complexe-significabile account of the object of assent and science, distinguish the habits of faith and theology, and deny that infused habits must be perceived. The answer is negative.
claims: A wayfarer cannot, under the present law, assent to theological truths without a special light.
Theological assent is identical with the theological proposition.
The object of science and assent is 'sic esse vel non esse'.
Faith and theology are distinct habits.

pg-b1q1.summary: Lectio 1, on Lombard's prologue. The exposition divides the prologue into Lombard's excuse, his rebuke of detractors, his commendation of the work by its four causes, and his exhortation to readers. The excuse is read as zeal for the Church overcoming diffidence before the arduous matter. The question then turns the prologue's theme of divine matter exceeding human capacity into an epistemological problem: can a wayfarer, without a special gift, scientifically assent to every supernatural truth? Gracilis answers that under the present law such assent requires a special light. He grounds this in a theory of assent: theological assent is the mental proposition itself, distinguished in species from a same-term non-assent, and its object is the complexe significabile 'sic esse vel non esse'. Theology without faith is not theology, a science is that by which things are known, and infused habits need not be perceived.
claims: Theological assent requires a special light under the present law.
Theological assent is identical with the mental proposition.
Lombard's work has God as principal and Lombard as instrumental cause.
